fact: LTCM ultimately lost $4.6 billion in 1998, and the private rescue was a $3.625 billion capital injection by a consortium of banks arranged under the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, announced in a statement by William J. McDonough.
Meriwether’s September 2, 1998 investor letter said the fund had suffered "a one-month loss of 44 percent" and disclosed that LTCM had been "severely impacted" by the market turmoil.

William J. McDonough said LTCM’s failure would have created a "severe liquidity problem" and that the Fed’s goal was to avoid a "fire sale" of positions that could "cause widespread disruption" in financial markets.

In 1998, LTCM had lost about $4.6 billion of its $4.7 billion capital base, and the rescue organized by the Federal Reserve Bank of New York was a $3.6 billion private-sector recapitalization by 14 banks on terms that gave creditors control of the fund.

LTCM built leverage through securities repurchase agreements and derivatives, and by early 1998 had more than $125 billion borrowed against about $5 billion in equity, with major Wall Street dealers and counterparties such as Goldman Sachs, Merrill Lynch, J.P. Morgan, and UBS extending financing and trading credit.

By late September 1998, LTCM had lost about 90% of its capital, and the Federal Reserve Bank of New York organized a $3.625 billion private rescue by 14 banks and securities firms to keep the fund from disorderly liquidation.
LTCM built leverage by borrowing heavily from major banks and using derivatives, and one account notes that UBS later wrote off $680 million after a special 1997 deal with LTCM to gain exposure.
At the end of 1997, LTCM returned $2-3/4 billion of capital to investors.
On September 23, 1998, the private sector parties arrived at an agreement providing a capital infusion of about $3-1/2 billion.
The $3-1/2 billion capital infusion was made in return for substantially diluting existing shareholders' stake in LTCM.

LTCM used a "market-neutral" relative-value/convergence strategy, exploiting temporary price differences between similar securities with long and offsetting short positions, and its documented net returns were 19.9% in 1994, 42.8% in 1995, 40.8% in 1996, and 17.1% in 1997.

John Meriwether’s Salomon Brothers experience and the 1991 Treasury auction scandal shaped LTCM by reinforcing his focus on trading relationships and risk controls after a desk scandal that ended his Salomon career.

After LTCM’s collapse, John Meriwether later launched JWM Partners, Myron Scholes remained active in finance and academia, and Robert C. Merton returned to academic and advisory roles; Meriwether also faced an SEC settlement and temporary suspension over the earlier Salomon scandal.

LTCM obtained extraordinary leverage by using securities repurchase agreements and derivatives, with major banks extending financing on very favorable terms and, in some cases, little or no initial margin.

At the September 1998 New York Fed rescue meeting, McDonough convened 14 major Wall Street firms and pressed them to form a private rescue consortium, warning that disorderly liquidation could destabilize markets.

John Meriwether relied heavily on Myron Scholes and Robert C. Merton’s quantitative models for LTCM’s relative-value trades, but the fund’s collapse exposed sharp disagreement over whether the models adequately captured rare market stress.

The full extent of LTCM’s counterparties’ exposures and some internal records remain disputed or not publicly disclosed, while the rescue consortium’s eventual wind-down terms were negotiated privately rather than released in a full public regulatory record.

LTCM used convergence trading in similar securities, relied on sophisticated mathematical models to exploit small pricing anomalies, and posted annualized returns of about 21% in 1994, 43% in 1995, 41% in 1996, and 17% in 1997.
John Meriwether was former Salomon Brothers vice chairman and head of fixed-income arbitrage, and he left after the Treasury-bond trading scandal at Salomon Brothers.

At the New York Fed rescue meetings in September 1998, William McDonough convened major banks and Wall Street firms, pressed them to form a private rescue, and the discussions centered on preventing a disorderly liquidation that could destabilize markets.

Meriwether’s September 1998 investor letter warned that LTCM had suffered enormous losses and said the fund was seeking a capital infusion, using unusually blunt language that has been widely quoted as admitting the firm had been hit by a 'severe liquidity crisis.'

William McDonough publicly justified the rescue as a private-sector solution to a private-sector problem, saying the creditors’ new equity infusion was preferable to a disorderly failure that could have forced fire sales and broader market disruption.

LTCM’s core early strategy was convergence trading—buying underpriced securities and shorting related overpriced ones, using quantitative models to exploit price deviations—and it reported annualized net returns of about 21% in 1994, 43% in 1995, and 41% in 1996.
John Meriwether’s Salomon Brothers background shaped LTCM’s culture: he imported a tight, elite trading partnership model built around quantitative risk-taking and recruited star academics to run it.

After LTCM collapsed, John Meriwether later founded another hedge fund, JWM Partners, while Robert C. Merton and Myron Scholes returned to academic and advisory careers; the collapse did not produce criminal convictions for the principals.
